header: \post{If You Demand Magic, Magic Won't Help}{Eliezer Yudkowsky}{2008}{https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/iiWiHgtQekWNnmE6Q/if-you-demand-magic-magic-won-t-help}
notes: \cpara{Pratchett's witches know that the gods exist, and so do not ``believe'' in them. The epigraph anticipates the post's claim that what is known to be real stops being an object of belief or longing.}
\cpara{Heads off the charge of not understanding fantasy by citing the author's upbringing, reading and writing.}
\cpara{The starting thought: if dragons were real and zebras unseen, fantasy would be about zebras. The epigraph makes the same point about gods.}
\cpara{Draws the moral as a proverb: ``The grass is always greener on the other side of unreality.''}
\cpara{Describes the plot the post will use: a sympathetic person from our world is carried into a world of magic and becomes a ``(superpowerful)'' sorcerer.}
\cpara{Sets out two premises, each qualified: readers ``Presumably'' imagine themselves as the protagonist, and, ``barring improbable demographics,'' most are not scientists.}
\cpara{The central question, left as a question. The next paragraph turns it into a claim, and states the claim as a condition.}

\cpara{The answer, in conditional form: without the capacity to be interested in real things, magic made real would lose ``the charm of unattainability.'' The post does not say how many readers meet the condition.}

\cfact{No source is given. The best-known study, by Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman (1978), found that 22 major winners ``were not happier than controls and took significantly less pleasure from a series of mundane events,'' which fits the post's point. I could read only its abstract, which gives no six-month figure and no measure of what the winners themselves had expected. A larger Swedish study (Lindqvist, \"Ostling and Cesarini, 2020) found winners' life satisfaction raised for more than a decade, with significantly smaller effects on happiness.}
\cpara{States the remedy: take joy in real things, in hang-gliding as much as in riding a dragon.}
\cpara{Disclaims any hostility to dragons.}
\cpara{Repeats the conditional of two paragraphs earlier, with hang-gliding and dragons.}
\cpara{Extends the argument from magic to the Future, granting that things ``do seem'' to be getting better.}
\cpara{Reminds the reader that the present is already the Future to people a thousand years ago, with opportunities ``undreamt-of even by kings.''}
\cpara{Applies the conditional to time: someone who cannot enjoy a Now will not be helped by a better one, since the Future will be another Now.}
\cpara{Anticipates the reply that a future pill could fix the problem, and says the point concerns which pills we should want.}

\cpara{Turns to a named commenter. The comment, on ``Reductionism'' (17 March 2008), matches the description: it cites protein folding and snowflake symmetry, and offers Rupert Sheldrake's account, in which structures arise ``through a repetition and reinforcement of habits.''}

\cpara{A claim about a named person's motives, stated as fact, with no evidence beyond the commenter's interest in the theory. The comment gives its own reason for that interest: that reductionism, in its words, ``is incapable of explaining the real world.''}
\cpara{A claim about the psychology of a whole community, with no evidence. It applies the post's thesis to New Agers; it is not a finding about them.}
\cpara{Raises the objection that the post is hostile to magic.}
\cpara{Answers that the target is a psychology, not magic: one that, in a world of spells, would pine for assembly lines.}
\cpara{Ties the post to ``Bind Yourself to Reality,'' posted the same day: part of that binding is accepting that ``you do live here.''}
\cpara{Offers the author's own case: no lack of ``dragons to fight, or magics to master'' in this world.}
\cpara{The thesis as a slogan: ``It's not where you are, it's who you are.''}
\cpara{Introduces a closing litany.}
\cpara{Six goals, each of which, the litany says, one may as well pursue in reality.}
